newsitem.title: BRAZIL: New corruption scandal rocks Brazil's Congress.
newsitem.headline: New corruption scandal rocks Brazil's Congress.

text.p: Brazil was rocked by a fresh corruption scandal Tuesday when a newspaper alleged five congressmen took bribes to vote in favor of a bill allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to stand for re-election.

Daily Folha de Sao Paulo published details of a taped telephone conversation attributed to Ronivon Santiago, a member of the Chamber of Deputies, and an unidentified person in which Santiago allegedly admitted to receiving $188,000 for his vote.

In the purported recordings, Santiago allegedly said the governors of Acre and Amazonas states, Oleir Cameli and Amazonino Mendes, also paid off another four deputies so they would vote in favor of the re-election bill.

None of the officials involved were immediately available for comment although Folha quoted three as denying the allegations. One deputy told the newspaper he was offered money, but said he did not take any.
The presidency did not have any immediate comment.

The legislation, which would also allow state governors and mayors to stand for a second consecutive term, was approved in two votes in the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress, in January.

It is currently in the Senate where a committee mulling the bill suspended its activities for 24 hours Tuesday amid an outcry over the Folha de Sao Paulo report. That committee earlier Tuesday rejected a motion to indefinitely suspend its deliberations.
Government-allied lawmakers sought to play down the alleged scandal.

"In no way is the government or the president involved in this. There is no indication that is the case," said Senator Sergio Machado, upper house leader of Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB).
But left-wing opposition parties said all further voting on the re-election bill should be suspended and called for a wide-ranging Commission of Parliamentary Inquiry (CPI) to investigate the report.

A CPI in the Senate is currently investigating an alleged, multi-million dollar scam involving municipal bonds, the latest in a string of corruption scandals to rock Congress since former president Fernando Collor stood down in disgrace in 1992.

"The re-election bill itself is now under suspicion. We believe it should be put on hold until the facts have been completely cleared up," said Jose Machado, leaders in the Chamber of Deputies of the leftist Workers Party (PT).

A Congress official said steps were being taken to set up an internal inquiry, often a first step in determining whether or not lawmakers accused of irregularities should be stripped of office. "Adequate measures are being taken," he said.

News of the report stung financial markets. The Sao Paulo stock exchange was down 0.41 percent at 10,637 points at 1245 local time/1545 GMT and Brazilian Brady bonds were also hit with C bonds 5/8 lower at 76-3/8 in London earlier.
The markets recovered somewhat later on. The Sao Paulo index recouped to trade up 0.33 percent at 10,716. The C bond later cut its losses to trade 1/4 lower at 76-3/4.
